methods.note: HotGauge methodology clearly described: perf-power-therm co-simulation integrating Sniper (performance), McPAT v1.2 (power), and 3D-ICE v3.0.0 (thermal). Hotspot detection algorithm detailed in Fig. 6 using local maxima candidate identification. Severity metric defined via three parameterized sigmoid functions (Eq. 2). Validation performed against Intel Core i5-10310U (14nm) and i7-1165G7 (10nm) via Intel TAT for Cdyn with reported errors 11% and 20% respectively.

code.note: GitHub repository URL (https://github.com/TuftsCompArchLab/HotGauge) and Zenodo DOI (10.5281/zenodo.5523504) provided in abstract and appendix, but actual code/scripts not accessible in supplied PDF pages. Appendix references README.md, docker_build.sh, docker_run.sh, and Python scripts (simulation_with_warmup.py) but no source code content supplied. Reproducibility hinges on external repository access unverified by this review.

parameters.note: Microarchitecture parameters fully specified in Table I: 7 cores, 224-entry ROB, 72 LQ, 56 SQ, 97 scheduler entries, L1I/L1D 32KiB each, L2 512KiB, L3 16MiB shared ring, 4-way associative. Frequency 5 GHz, voltage 1.4 V. Thermal stack parameters in Table II: silicon 380 µm (1.2e-4 W/µm K), solder TIM 200 µm (0.25e-4), copper heat spreader 3000 µm (3.9e-4), thermal grease 30 µm (0.04e-4). Hotspot definition parameters: Tth=80°C, MLTDth=25°C, radius=1mm. Severity sigmoid parameters explicitly given in Eq. 2: σdf=(115,0,0.2,2), σM=(15,-0.25,0.2,1.25), σT=(60,0.35,0.05,0.65).

config.note: Paper claims 50% area scaling per technology node (14nm→10nm→7nm) with constant floorplan layout, but critical contradiction emerges: Section III-E states 'global wires do not scale very well across technology nodes and die-size has historically remained constant' yet Table I shows Core area reducing 5mm²→2.5mm²→1.25mm². Floorplan Fig. 5 (7nm) provided as schematic only without detailed block coordinates; functional units enumerated (cALU, fpIWin, RATs, RFs, ROB, core_other, AVX512) but relative positions and exact power distributions per unit unspecified. McPAT configuration file (XML config) not disclosed—only statement that model uses 'highest granularity setting'. Thermal stack model states 'active layer' separated from 'bulk die' to improve accuracy, but exact layer boundaries and node spacing discrepancies not quantified. Heatsink model HS483-ND/P14752-ND held constant across nodes despite die area reduction, increasing Ψ from 0.96 to 1.40 °C/W (Table IV); this physical inconsistency acknowledged but not addressed.

data.note: Cdyn validation against real silicon available only for 14nm (error 11% avg) and 10nm (error 20% avg) via Intel TAT on limited SPEC2006 subset (bzip2, gcc, omnetpp, povray, hmmer). 7nm model entirely extrapolated using 'standard transistor scaling trends' with no published silicon validation. Paper acknowledges in Section III-D: 'It is not possible to capture all circuit design characteristics in a high-level power model such as McPAT and more importantly it is the general scaling trends that we are trying to capture.' TUH results (Fig. 10-11) show ≥2× variation between 14nm and 7nm and >100× variation across benchmarks (0.2–150 ms), but individual power traces per functional unit not reported—only aggregate McPAT output. Temperature initialization ('non-uniform temperature initialization' Section III-C) modeled qualitatively via idle OS workload trace but exact thermal state prior to ROI execution unknown. Workload selection limited to SPEC2006 single-threaded on single core; multi-threaded behavior and SMT contention effects unstudied despite SMT capability modeled in Table I.

findings.reason: Table I specifies 50% area scaling per node (5→2.5→1.25 mm²), but Section III-E acknowledges global wires do not scale proportionally and die size historically constant. This creates internal contradiction: if die size stays constant, how can core area scale uniformly while maintaining realistic power density and thermal behavior? Paper provides no resolution.
findings.locator: Table I (Core area [mm²] row) vs Section III-E (paragraph 1) vs Section III: 'approximately a 5mm² die'

findings.reason: Cdyn validation performed only on real 14nm silicon (i5-10310U, 11% error) and 10nm silicon (i7-1165G7, 20% error). 7nm model is pure extrapolation using 'standard transistor scaling trends' with 20% Cdyn reduction per node—no actual silicon validation provided. Case study conclusions rest on unvalidated 7nm power estimates.
findings.locator: Section III-D, Table III (validation error 20% for 10nm is highest), and Section III-B ('Using standard transistor scaling trends, we tune leakage, dynamic power, and area')

findings.reason: Figure 5 shows 7nm core floorplan as labeled schematic only, with no absolute coordinates, block dimensions in mm, or power dissipation values per unit. McPAT config file structure not disclosed. Paper claims 50 functional units modeled (Section II-C) vs 6 in HotSniper, but explicit list and spatial placement unavailable.
findings.locator: Figure 5 caption ('The floorplan of each core used in this case study') and Section III-C statement '50 units' versus Fig. 5 visual representation

findings.reason: Paper states IC 'further divided in the vertical direction between the active layer and the bulk of the die' to improve thermal accuracy (Section III-C), but exact layer boundaries, node spacing in vertical vs horizontal directions, and quantified discrepancy resolution not provided. Affects hotspot localization accuracy.
findings.locator: Section III-C: 'This was done to increase the resolution and accuracy of the thermal model within the die, which is essential for realistically modeling hotspots. Thermal simulations without these added layers resulted in scenarios where heat spread more horizontally and less vertically than expected.'

findings.reason: Identical HS483-ND heatsink model used across all three process nodes despite die area reduction of 75% (14nm→7nm). Thermal resistance Ψ increases from 0.96 to 1.40 °C/W (Table IV), indicating smaller die dissipates heat less efficiently through same heatsink. This mismatch is acknowledged ('the IC is smaller, resulting in a higher thermal resistance') but unresolved—no sensitivity analysis on heatsink scaling impact.
findings.locator: Table II caption ('heatsink model... HS483-ND') and Table IV discussion; Section III-E footnote 3

findings.reason: Non-uniform temperature initialization simulated via 'idle background task thermal warm-up trace' (Section III-C, Fig. 8) but exact trace and warm-up duration not specified. Real processor background thermal state prior to SPEC2006 ROI unknown and inferred.
findings.locator: Section III-C: 'we make our own additions: thermal and floorplan models for AVX512... non-uniform temperature initialization of the thermal stack in 3D-ICE to model the fact that CPUs have other workloads'

findings.reason: Case study uses only single-threaded SPEC2006 on single core. SMT (2 threads/core) and L3 contention capability modeled in Table I but not exercised in primary results (Section IV). Multi-threaded hotspot behavior and inter-core thermal coupling unstudied.
findings.locator: Section III: 'The single-threaded version of each workload was run on a single core' and Table I 'SMT: 2' but no multi-threaded results reported in Section IV

findings.reason: TUH varies >100× across benchmarks (0.2–150 ms, Section IV-C) and ≥2× between 14nm and 7nm, but underlying cause analysis shallow. Figure 11 shows gobmk TUH order-of-magnitude spread across cores but causal mechanism (power profile, memory behavior, instruction mix) not investigated.
findings.locator: Section IV-C: 'We observe greater than 2 orders of magnitude difference in TUH across SPEC2006 benchmarks—anywhere from 0.2 ms to 150 ms' without detailed power/performance mechanism analysis

findings.reason: Section IV-D and Figure 12 show hotspot locations (cALU, fpIWin, RATs, RFs, ROB, core_other) aggregated over SPEC2006. Paper acknowledges (Section IV-D): 'If AVX-intensive benchmarks were selected, we would see a high volume of hotspots in the AVX unit' and 'Understanding the behavior of hotspots—particularly related to specialized units...is part of our future work plan.' Case study generalizability limited.
findings.locator: Section IV-D: 'While the primary locations of hotspots for this particular work-load were..., other units also manifest hotspots.'

findings.reason: Section V-A (Figure 13) demonstrates that 10× scaling of fpIWin does not reduce 7nm hotspot severity below 14nm baseline for gcc, and effectiveness varies wildly across benchmarks (milc benefits more from RF scaling). Section V-B shows 75–150% uniform IC area scaling required—a 'limit test' revealing static floorplanning cannot solve problem. However, alternative dynamic or architecture-level mitigation techniques mentioned as 'ongoing work' and not detailed.
findings.locator: Section V-A: 'even when the fpIWin is scaled by a factor of 10×, the hotspot severity in the fpIWin unit of the 7nm processor is still higher than in the 14nm part' and Section V-B: 'the area of the 7nm IC would need to be increased by between 75% and 150%'

findings.reason: GitHub URL and Zenodo DOI cited in abstract and appendix, but source code, data, and reproducibility artifacts not included in supplied PDF. Appendix B lists Zenodo DOI 5523504 and 5523535 (noted as alternate) but accessibility and completeness of archived artifacts not verified.
findings.locator: Abstract: 'https://github.com/TuftsCompArchLab/HotGauge and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5523504' and Appendix B 'Zenodo DOI 5523504' vs 'Zenodo DOI 5523535'

findings.reason: Equation 2 sigmoid parameters (σdf, σM, σT) stated as 'a contribution for the case study, are fitted from industry data and insight' (Section III-G) but exact calibration methodology, source industry data, and sensitivity analysis not disclosed. Metric thresholds (Tth=80°C, critical severity=0.5) described as 'tunable' but no parametric sweep study provided.
findings.locator: Section III-G: 'The parameters here, a contribution for the case study, are fitted from industry data and insight.' and Section III-G: 'HotGauge is a tunable framework so this definition can be tuned by the designer'

findings.reason: Paper emphasizes 'transient thermal simulation' and short time constants (0.2–0.6 ms TUH) vs traditional steady-state approaches. However, simulation window of 200M instructions (Section III-A) duration not explicitly stated in wall-clock time; with 5 GHz frequency, this spans 40 ms, but thermal transient duration relative to workload steady-state behavior not delineated.
findings.locator: Section III-A: 'we simulate each workload's region of interest(roi) for 200M instructions, using a time step of 1M cycles. This is sufficient for transient thermal simulations since we are interested in hotspot behavior which has very short time scales' (duration not quantified)

findings.reason: Cache warm-up performed before ROI (Section III-A) but exact duration and thermal state post-warmup vs cold-start not distinguished in results until Section IV-A (Figures 8a–8b). TUH variation due to cache warm-up effects conflated with technology node effects in main results presentation.
findings.locator: Section III-A: 'cache warm-up is always performed' vs Section IV-A: 'After an idle warmup, not only is there increased variation...a threshold of 110°C is surpassed more than 4× faster' (separate analysis from main TUH reporting)

findings.reason: Section II-A claims 'power density greater than 8 W/mm² running bzip2 with 1 thread' but this appears to be peak/localized value not clearly distinguished from average. Aggregate chip power and per-unit power distribution across functional units not disclosed, hampering independent verification of hotspot severity scaling.
findings.locator: Section II-A: 'Critically, we observe power density greater than 8 W/mm2 running bzip2 with 1 thread. This power density is approximately 2× the power density of what could have been expected if Dennard scaling were still in effect.'
